title: GPX Route Count Tool: Count Routes in a File
description: Count the route elements in a GPX file with the GPX Route Count Tool — how many planned routes a document actually carries. Free, local.
summary_sentence: For example, an export that claims to hold 'the route' may carry three <rte> elements — the original, last year's variant and an accidental duplicate — and this tool counts all three.
quick_answer: The GPX Route Count Tool counts the route (<rte>) elements inside a GPX file. Load the file locally and read how many planned routes the document actually carries — the structural fact that explains duplicate lines on maps, confused imports and libraries that never match their inventories.
steps_intro: One element per route — count them before the map draws them on top of each other:

body.t: A platform shows your route twice. Either the file carries two routes or the platform duplicated it — the count settles which, alongside the
's census of the points inside them.
A folder of route files becomes a catalogue once each file's route count is known — files with zero routes are recordings in disguise, files with five are bundles.
Merged two route files? The union's count should equal the sum of the sources — the
Event and tour operators ship one GPX with every day's route inside. Counting the routes is step one of unpacking the bundle.

A file with 2 <trk> and 3 <rte> carries two journeys actually travelled and three plans. The counts sound similar and mean opposite things — plans propose, tracks testify — and confusing them corrupts training logs.
A count of zero in a file named 'route.gpx' means the export saved the recording instead — a naming lie the count exposes in one second, before you navigate a plan that does not exist.

popular_table.title: What gets counted
popular_table.intro: The document's route layer, distinguished from its neighbours.
popular_table.note: A route's identity is its element, not its name — two routes may share a name and still be two routes, which is exactly the duplication this count reveals.

faq: Does a route with zero points count?
Yes — an empty <rte> is still an element the file carries (and a smell worth investigating). Structure counts what is there, not what is useful.
Names are optional in the schema; the count does not care. Unnamed routes are how bundles hide extra days.
Courses are usually exported as tracks or single routes; a course bundle with several <rte> elements is precisely the case this count clarifies.
Can it list the routes' names too?
The count is the headline; names ride inside the elements for any XML reader to list. The census mindset is this family's: count first, inspect second.
Why would a planner export duplicates?
Edits saved as new routes instead of replacing, variants kept 'just in case', exports appended rather than overwritten — ordinary software behaviour, visible only when you count.
A converted track often arrives as one route with thousands of rtept — the count says 1 route while the point counter explains the file's size.
